proofs.proof_tex:
The off-gate interval always covers the target.  Indeed, the bounded-entry and strong-spectrum assumptions give
\[
|\theta_n|
\le\|u\|_2\|A^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|v\|_2
\le (B\sqrt n){1\over cn}(B\sqrt n)
={B^2\over c}=M_0.
\tag{1}
\]
On \(G_n\), condition on \(X\).  By the established conditional-reduction lemma, \(Z_n=m_n+\xi_n\) with \(\xi_n\sim N(0,I_{2r})\), the donor-conditional target is \(\theta_{X,n}=\sigma^2m_{p,n}^{\mathsf T}D_nm_{q,n}\), and
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}
P\bigl(|\theta_{X,n}-\theta_n|>d_n,\,G_n\bigr)
\le e^{-n/2}+3(e+n)^{-6}.
\tag{2}
\]
The established Gaussian-outer-inversion lemma, applied conditionally for the realized invertible \(D_n\), shows that
\[
P\left(
|\widehat\theta_n-\theta_{X,n}|>\sigma^2W_n
\,\middle|\,X\right)\le\alpha
\quad\hbox{on \(G_n\)}.
\tag{3}
\]
If neither event in (2)--(3) occurs, then the triangle inequality yields
\[
|\widehat\theta_n-\theta_n|
\le\sigma^2W_n+d_n,
\]
so the on-gate interval covers \(\theta_n\).  Together with (1),
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}P\{\theta_n\notin I_n^{\mathrm{out}}\}
\le\alpha+e^{-n/2}+3(e+n)^{-6}.
\tag{4}
\]
Taking the limit superior in (4) proves the uniform coverage assertion.  No step divides by \(u\), \(v\), or either loading norm.

For the comparison clause, the class-embedding proposition proves that \(\mathcal P_n\) is a canonical bounded square one-target subclass satisfying Yan--Wainwright conditions \(4.1\)--\(4.4\mathrm{b}\) for large \(n\).  The cited Yan--Wainwright condition lemma records that their Gaussian theorem also assumes \(4.4\mathrm{c}\).  If \(u=v=0\), the law remains in \(\mathcal P_n\), (4) still applies, and the embedding proposition proves that \(4.4\mathrm{c}\) fails.  Hence our coverage guarantee includes points outside the loading-restricted theorem's scope within this embedded subclass.  This establishes precisely the stated subclass extension and nothing about points in the full published class outside the embedding.

Put \(\delta=2^{-p_n-1}\), and let \(\mathcal B\) be the coordinate box of radius \(\delta\) about the exact dyadic arrays.  All public controls have zero input radius by the theorem's exact-dyadic premise.  We construct both a coarse branch and a sharp branch.

Let \(T\) be a directed upper bound for every absolute coordinate over \(\mathcal B\).  At any point of \(\mathcal B\) where \(G_n\) holds,
\[
\|X_r^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le{2\over cn},
\quad
\|Z_{p,n}\|_2,\|Z_{q,n}\|_2
\le{\sqrt nT\over\sigma}.
\tag{1}
\]
The first inequality is the on-gate lower singular-value bound; the other two follow from orthonormality of the retained projectors.  Hence
\[
t_{Z,n}\le{\sqrt{2n}T\over\sigma}=:\overline t.
\tag{2}
\]
Since \(\beta_\alpha(t)=\alpha/[4(1+t)]\), the definition of \(\zeta_\alpha\) and monotonicity of \(\Phi^{-1}\) give
\[
0<\zeta_\alpha(t)\le z_{\max}:=\Phi^{-1}(1-3\alpha/8).
\tag{3}
\]
Define
\[
\overline R=\sqrt{C_{r,\alpha}\log(e+2\overline t+A_{r,\alpha})}
\]
and
\[
\overline W={2\over cn}
\left\{z_{\max}(\overline t+\overline R)
+{C_{r,\alpha}\over2}\log(e+\overline t+\overline R)\right\}.
\tag{4}
\]
Equations (1)--(3) and the analytic-half-width definition imply \(W_n\le\overline W\).  Moreover,
\[
|\widehat\theta_n|=|RX_r^+C|\le{2T^2\over c},
\tag{5}
\]
and the donor-allowance definition gives
\[
d_n\le K_0\sigma^2\ell_n n^{-2}
\left({\sqrt nT\over\sigma}+\sqrt{\ell_n}\right)^2=:\overline d.
\tag{6}
\]
Thus every feasible on-gate interval is contained in
\[
[-\overline H,\overline H],
\qquad
\overline H={2T^2\over c}+\sigma^2\overline W+\overline d,
\tag{7}
\]
whereas every off-gate interval equals \([-M_0,M_0]\).  Directed majorants of (1)--(7) are finite and computable; for a coarse polynomial bound one may use \(\log(e+x)\le1+x\) and \(\sqrt x\le1+x\).  Their exponent encodings have polynomial length because the arithmetic model has arbitrary-precision signed exponents.  The hull of (7) and the off-gate interval is therefore a computable enclosure independent of any spectral gap.

For the sharp branch use \(\tau=(cn/2)^2\) and the projectors
\[
P_R={\bf1}_{(\tau,\infty)}(X^{\mathsf T}X),
\qquad
P_L={\bf1}_{(\tau,\infty)}(XX^{\mathsf T}).
\tag{8}
\]
When the certified count above \(\tau\) is \(r\),
\[
X_r=P_LXP_R,
\qquad
X_r^+=X_r^{\mathsf T}(X_rX_r^{\mathsf T}+I-P_L)^{-1}.
\tag{9}
\]
To verify (9), use a compact SVD \(X_r=U_rS_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\).  The inverse in (9) is \(U_rS_r^{-2}U_r^{\mathsf T}+I-P_L\), and multiplication by \(X_r^{\mathsf T}\) gives \(V_rS_r^{-1}U_r^{\mathsf T}\).

Compute (8) from the matrix-sign iteration in the certified-handle definition.  The certified-error-recurrence lemma proves both its enclosure validity and the residual-certified validity of every inverse in (9).  It also proves that, on a stable spectral box, the sign iteration reaches the sharp branch in \(O(\log(q_n+2))\) iterations and that repeated singular values within the retained cluster do not matter.  The exact interval depends only on the invariant quantities
\[
\widehat\theta_n=RX_r^+C,
\quad
s_{Z,n}={1\over\sigma}
\sqrt{\|X_r^+C\|_2^2+
\|(X_r^+)^{\mathsf T}R^{\mathsf T}\|_2^2},
\tag{10}
\]
\[
\|Z_{p,n}\|_2={\|P_RR^{\mathsf T}\|_2\over\sigma},
\qquad
\|Z_{q,n}\|_2={\|P_LC\|_2\over\sigma}.
\tag{11}
\]
Thus a change of basis inside a repeated retained singular subspace changes no endpoint.  A tie across the retained--discarded boundary is not accepted and invokes the coarse hull.

For scalar functions, binary range reduction and the exponential series give directed intervals.  In particular, for \(m\ge0\), Taylor's formula obtained by repeated integration yields
\[
\left|e^y-\sum_{j=0}^m{y^j\over j!}\right|
\le {e^{|y|}|y|^{m+1}\over(m+1)!}.
\tag{12}
\]
The identities
\[
\Phi(x)={1\over2}+{1\over\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_0^x e^{-t^2/2}\,dt
\tag{13}
\]
and, because \(2r\) is an even integer,
\[
F_{\chi^2_{2r}}(x)
=1-e^{-x/2}\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}{(x/2)^j\over j!},
\qquad x\ge0,
\tag{14}
\]
therefore admit directed rational evaluation to \(s\) bits in time polynomial in \(s\) and the argument's bit length.  The Gaussian moment calculation
\[
P(Z\ge x)\le\inf_{t>0}e^{-tx+t^2/2}=e^{-x^2/2}
\tag{15}
\]
provides a normal-quantile bracket of polynomial bit length.  Formula (14) provides a chi-square bracket of size \(O_{r_0}(1+\log(1/\gamma))\) at upper-tail probability \(\gamma\).  The densities are positive on finite interior brackets.  Directed bisection, making a comparison only when the distribution-function enclosure separates the target probability, therefore returns an interval containing the quantile \(Q\) with width at most
\[
8\,2^{1-q_n}(1+|Q|).
\tag{16}
\]
Because \(r\le r_0\) is fixed and the public controls are exact dyadics, the number and cost of the bisection and function-evaluation steps are polynomial in \(q_n,L_n\), and \(\lceil\log_2(1/\alpha)\rceil\).

Choose a deterministic precision cap
\[
q_n^\star=8\bigl(n+L_n+p_n+\lceil\log_2(1/\alpha)\rceil+1\bigr)^2.
\tag{17}
\]
At doubled precisions no larger than (17), attempt to certify that the whole box is off the gate or that it is on the gate with a common split (8).  If either attempt succeeds, use its certified branch.  If neither succeeds at the cap, return the coarse hull (7).  Hence the procedure always terminates after \(O(\log q_n^\star)\) attempts.  Each attempt has a polynomial number of matrix operations; matrix-sign iteration is capped by the count in the recurrence lemma; residual inversion and scalar bisection have polynomial cost by (1)--(16).  Mantissas have at most \(q_n^\star\) bits and dynamically stored exponents have polynomial encoding length.  Thus the total bit complexity is polynomial in the quantities stated in the theorem.

Finally fix \((X,R,C)\in\mathcal B\), write its exact interval as \([L,U]\), and write the returned interval as \([\underline L,\overline U]\).  The recurrence lemma, residual bound, quantile bracketing, and branch-hull rule prove
\[
\underline L\le L\le U\le\overline U.
\tag{18}
\]
By the definitions of the two recorded radii, endpointwise propagation gives
\[
0\le L-\underline L\le\Delta_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+\Delta_n^{\mathrm{arith}},
\qquad
0\le\overline U-U\le\Delta_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+\Delta_n^{\mathrm{arith}}.
\tag{19}
\]
Adding (19) proves the claimed factor-two length bound.  Arbitrary-precision signed exponents exclude overflow and subnormals in the abstract model.  The stated IEEE branch emits no certificate if rescaling and exponent widening fail to exclude overflow, subnormal values, or flushing.  This completes all deterministic claims.

If a later corollary replaces an exact control by a returned certified interval, the recurrence lemma proves containment after half the interval width is inserted as input radius.  Since the cost and output size of obtaining that interval are not bounded by its original description alone, the theorem correctly makes no polynomial-complexity claim without a supplied uniform modulus.

On \(\kappa_n=0\), every point of \(\mathcal B_n\) has coordinate magnitude at most \(T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+1\).  The coarse construction (1)--(7) in the deterministic-certificate proof bounds the center, half-width, donor allowance, and branch hull by a fixed polynomial in
\[
n+T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+\alpha^{-1}+1.
\tag{1}
\]
The fallback radius \(M_0=B^2/c\) is fixed.  The handle may choose every recorded radius no larger than the diameter of that coarse hull plus one outward rounding unit.  Increasing fixed constants once proves the first inequality.

Now impose the three stable spectral inequalities.  With \(\tau=(cn/2)^2\), the retained and discarded squared singular values are separated from \(\tau\) by at least
\[
\min\left\{(3cn/4)^2-(cn/2)^2,
(cn/2)^2-(cn/4)^2\right\}
={3c^2n^2\over16}.
\tag{2}
\]
Thus the stable-box part of the certified-error-recurrence lemma applies.  It proves, from the explicit matrix-sign, residual-inversion, product, scalar, quantile, wrapping, and branching recurrences, that the sharp branch is certified and that each endpoint radius is at most
\[
K_\star(n+T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+\alpha^{-1}+1)^{k_\star}
\bigl(2^{-p_n}+2^{1-q_n}\bigr).
\tag{3}
\]
The lower bound \(s_r(X')\ge3cn/4\) justifies every inversion; the discarded upper bound certifies the rank split; and the largest-singular-value bound controls every intermediate magnitude.  No individual singular vector is selected, so repeated retained singular values are allowed.  Exact-dyadic public controls contribute zero initial radius.

By construction, \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{enc}}\) is the sum of the endpoint radii attributable to the coordinate boxes and \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{arith}}\) is the sum attributable to directed arithmetic and certified branching.  The recurrence has only a fixed number of endpoint stages and \(O(\log(q_n+2))\) sign stages; its stable proof absorbs their polynomial count into \(K_\star,k_\star\).  Hence their sum satisfies (3).  Every recorded summand is nonnegative and no larger than the sum, which proves the last assertion.

First, the schedule gives
\[
T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}
=2^{L_n-p_n-\lceil\log_2(p_n+2)\rceil-4}
=2^{\lceil\log_2\tau_n\rceil+2g_n+C_\star-4}
\ge\tau_n
\tag{1}
\]
when \(C_\star\ge4\).  For fixed public controls it is polynomial in \(n\), and \(p_n,q_n,L_n\) have the stated polynomial bit bounds.  On \(\kappa_n=0\), rounding a coordinate produces a numerator with at most
\[
p_n+\lceil\log_2(T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+1)\rceil+2
\]
bits, while the signed exponent \(-p_n\) has \(O(\log(p_n+2))\) bits.  A sufficiently large fixed \(C_\star\) therefore places every rounded coordinate and every fixed exact-dyadic public control in the directed-rounding input model.

There are \(N_n=n^2+2n\le3n^2\) observed coordinates, and every mean coordinate is bounded by \(B\).  If \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), exponential Markov inequalities give
\[
P(|Z|>x)\le2e^{-x^2/2},\qquad x\ge0.
\tag{2}
\]
Since (1) implies \(T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}\ge B+\sigma\sqrt{12\log(e+n)}+1\), a union bound gives
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}P(\kappa_n=1)
\le2N_ne^{-6\log(e+n)}
\le6n^2(e+n)^{-6}=O(n^{-4})=o(n^{-1}).
\tag{3}
\]

We next bound spectral failure directly.  A maximal \(1/4\)-separated subset of the Euclidean unit sphere has at most \(9^n\) points, by comparing disjoint radius-\(1/8\) balls with the radius-\(9/8\) ball.  For two such nets, approximation of both unit vectors gives
\[
\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le2\max_{x,y\text{ in the nets}}|x^{\mathsf T}Ey|.
\]
Each \(x^{\mathsf T}Ey/\sigma\) is standard normal under the Gaussian-block assumption.  Equation (2) and a union bound imply, for some fixed \(k_0>0\) and all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}
P\{\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}>cn/8\}
\le2\,9^{2n}\exp\left(-{c^2n^2\over512\sigma^2}\right)
\le e^{-k_0n^2}.
\tag{4}
\]
The singular-value min--max formula and the triangle inequality imply
\[
|s_j(A+E)-s_j(A)|\le\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\tag{5}
\]
On the complement of the event in (4), (5) and the exact-rank and strong-spectrum assumptions give
\[
s_r(X)\ge7cn/8,\qquad s_{r+1}(X)\le cn/8,\qquad
s_1(X)\le C_0n+cn/8.
\tag{6}
\]
The true donor and every point in its encoding box differ entrywise by at most \(2^{-p_n}\), hence in operator norm by at most \(n2^{-p_n}\).  Therefore, for all sufficiently large \(n\), every donor in that box satisfies
\[
s_r\ge3cn/4,\qquad s_{r+1}\le cn/4,\qquad
s_1\le3C_0n/2.
\tag{7}
\]

Let
\[
P_n^\star=K_\star(n+T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+\alpha^{-1}+1)^{k_\star}.
\]
On \(\kappa_n=0\), the coordinate box is bounded by \(T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+1\).  The stable-padding lemma, (4), and (7) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}
\mathbb E_P[&(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+\Delta_n^{\mathrm{arith}})
\mathbf1\{\kappa_n=0\}]\\
&\le P_n^\star(2^{-p_n}+2^{1-q_n})
+P_n^\star e^{-k_0n^2}=o(n^{-m})
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
for every fixed \(m>0\).  Indeed, for fixed \(\alpha\), (1) makes \(T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}\) and \(P_n^\star\) polynomial in \(n\), whereas \(p_n=n^2+O(\log n)\) and \(q_n=n^2+O(\log n)\).  Since all recorded radii are nonnegative, (8) also holds for every individual summand.

The corrected deterministic certificate applies because the controls are exact dyadics.  On \(\kappa_n=0\), it gives
\[
I_n^{\mathrm{out}}(X,R,C)\subseteq I_n^{\mathrm{fp}},
\qquad
0\le\varepsilon_n
\le2(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+\Delta_n^{\mathrm{arith}})
=2\Delta_n^{\mathrm{num}}.
\tag{9}
\]
On \(\kappa_n=1\), the composed procedure returns \([-M_0,M_0]\).  This contains the target because
\[
|\theta_n|
\le\|u\|_2\|A^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|v\|_2
\le(B\sqrt n){1\over cn}(B\sqrt n)=M_0.
\tag{10}
\]
Also \(0\le\varepsilon_n\le2M_0\) on this branch.  Equations (3), (8), and (9) therefore imply
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}\mathbb E_P[\varepsilon_n]=o(n^{-1}),
\qquad
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}
\mathbb E_P[M_0\mathbf1\{\kappa_n=1\}]=o(n^{-1}),
\tag{11}
\]
as well as the summand-by-summand claim.

Pointwise, (9)--(10) imply
\[
\{\theta_n\in I_n^{\mathrm{out}}\}
\subseteq\{\theta_n\in I_n^{\mathrm{fp}}\}.
\]
The established uniform-coverage theorem for \(I_n^{\mathrm{out}}\) proves the asserted coverage for \(I_n^{\mathrm{fp}}\).  Moreover,
\[
w_n\ge b_n=\sigma^2\|A^+\|_{\mathrm F}
\ge{\sigma^2\over s_1(A)}
\ge{\sigma^2\over C_0n}.
\tag{12}
\]
Combining (11)--(12) gives
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}{\mathbb E_P[\varepsilon_n]\over w_n}
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{13}
\]
For nonnegative \(x,y\), \(x\le y+[x-y]_+\).  Hence
\[
\operatorname{length}(I_n^{\mathrm{fp}})
\le\operatorname{length}(I_n^{\mathrm{out}})+\varepsilon_n.
\]
The established transition-length theorem and (13) prove the claimed expected-length bound.

Finally suppose \(b_n/a_n\to0\).  Equation (12) implies
\[
na_n\ge {\sigma^2\over C_0}{a_n\over b_n}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
By (11),
\[
{\mathbb E_{P_n}[\varepsilon_n]\over a_n}
={n\mathbb E_{P_n}[\varepsilon_n]\over na_n}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{14}
\]
Thus \(\varepsilon_n/a_n\to0\) in \(L^1(P_n)\) and in probability.  On \(\kappa_n=0\), (9) makes the length difference nonnegative and at most \(\varepsilon_n\); on \(\kappa_n=1\), the exceptional probability tends to zero by (3).  Therefore
\[
{\operatorname{length}(I_n^{\mathrm{fp}})
-\operatorname{length}(I_n^{\mathrm{out}})\over a_n}
\longrightarrow0
\quad\hbox{in probability}.
\tag{15}
\]
The established oracle-length theorem for \(I_n^{\mathrm{out}}\), followed by (15), proves the oracle Gaussian ratio for \(I_n^{\mathrm{fp}}\).  At \(r=1,u=v=0\), (12) shows that the statistical width is of order at least \(n^{-1}\), while (8) and (11) give \(o(n^{-1})\) for every numerical component.  This verifies the advertised joint-zero boundary case.  The last sentence follows because the recurrence controls correctness for a supplied interval but, absent a known modulus, cannot bound the cost or output size of querying an arbitrary name.

added_lemmas.statement: For every \(P\in\mathcal P_n\), the augmented mean \(\overline M_n\) has rank \(r\) and, with donor dimensions \(N_1=T_1=n\) and target dimensions \(N_2=T_2=1\), its three observed blocks have exactly the law of \((X,C,R)\).  This is a square one-target bounded Gaussian subclass of the Yan--Wainwright four-block model.  For every fixed positive approximation tolerance, their conditions \(4.1\), \(4.2\), \(4.3\), and \(4.4\mathrm{a}\)--\(4.4\mathrm{b}\) hold for all sufficiently large \(n\), uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_n\).  At \(u=v=0\), their condition \(4.4\mathrm{c}\) fails.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix \(P=P_{A,u,v}\in\mathcal P_n\).  By the exact-rank and strong-spectrum assumptions, write
\[
A=USV^{\mathsf T},\qquad cn\le s_r(A)\le s_1(A)\le C_0n.
\tag{1}
\]
The row-span and column-span assumptions give \(u=uVV^{\mathsf T}\) and \(v=UU^{\mathsf T}v\).  Define
\[
L=\begin{bmatrix}U\\ uVS^{-1}\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
H=\begin{bmatrix}V\\ v^{\mathsf T}US^{-1}\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Direct block multiplication and the definition \(\theta_n=uA^+v=uVS^{-1}U^{\mathsf T}v\) yield
\[
LSH^{\mathsf T}
=\begin{bmatrix}
USV^{\mathsf T}&UU^{\mathsf T}v\\
uVV^{\mathsf T}&uVS^{-1}U^{\mathsf T}v
\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}A&v\\u&\theta_n\end{bmatrix}
=\overline M_n.
\tag{2}
\]
Both \(L\) and \(H\) have full column rank because their first \(n\) rows are \(U\) and \(V\), respectively.  Since \(S\) is invertible, (2) proves \(\operatorname{rank}(\overline M_n)=r\).  Under the Gaussian-block assumption, the upper-left, upper-right, and lower-left observed blocks of the corresponding four-block observation are \(A+E=X\), \(v+f=C\), and \(u+e=R\), with mutually independent \(N(0,\sigma^2)\) entry noise.  The lower-right block is the single missing target.  Thus the observation law is exactly the claimed square four-block law with \(N=T=n+1\), \(N_1=T_1=n\), and \(N_2=T_2=1\).

We next check the displayed Yan--Wainwright conditions in their own notation; see equations \(4.1\)--\(4.4\) of Yan and Wainwright~\cite{YanWainwright2024}.  Put
\[
\ell=S^{-1}V^{\mathsf T}u^{\mathsf T},
\qquad q=S^{-1}U^{\mathsf T}v.
\]
The bounded-entry and strong-spectrum assumptions imply
\[
\|\ell\|_2\le {\|u\|_2\over s_r(A)}
\le {B\over c\sqrt n},
\qquad
\|q\|_2\le {B\over c\sqrt n}.
\tag{3}
\]
The left singular space of \(\overline M_n\) is \(\operatorname{col}(L)\).  Hence an orthonormal basis of that space has the form
\[
\overline U=L(L^{\mathsf T}L)^{-1/2}O_L,
\]
for an orthogonal \(r\)-by-\(r\) matrix \(O_L\).  If \(\overline U_1\) denotes its first \(n\) rows, then
\[
\overline U_1^{\mathsf T}\overline U_1
=O_L^{\mathsf T}(I_r+\ell\ell^{\mathsf T})^{-1}O_L.
\tag{4}
\]
Thus (3) gives, uniformly over the class and for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
{1\over2}I_r\preceq
\overline U_1^{\mathsf T}\overline U_1\preceq I_r.
\tag{5}
\]
The identical argument with \(H\) and \(q\) gives (5) for the first \(n\) rows \(\overline V_1\) of the right singular-vector matrix.  Since \(n/(n+1)\in[1/2,1]\), these inequalities verify condition \(4.1\), for example with fixed constants \(c_\ell=1/2\) and \(c_u=2\).

Deleting the last row and column is multiplication by coordinate contractions.  The singular-value min--max formula therefore gives
\[
s_r(\overline M_n)\ge s_r(A)\ge cn.
\tag{6}
\]
In Yan--Wainwright notation, \(\omega=\sigma\) and \(\sigma_r^\star=s_r(\overline M_n)\).  Consequently their noise functional in \(4.2\) obeys
\[
\rho_{N,T}
={\omega\over\sigma_r^\star\sqrt{\min\{N_1,T_1\}}}
\le {\sigma\over c n^{3/2}}.
\tag{7}
\]
For fixed \(r\le r_0\),
\[
\rho_{N,T}\sqrt{r+\log(N+T)}
\le {\sigma\sqrt{r_0+\log(2n+2)}\over c n^{3/2}}
\longrightarrow0,
\tag{8}
\]
which verifies \(4.3\) for every fixed positive tolerance and all sufficiently large \(n\).  The auxiliary noise levels in \(4.4\) satisfy
\[
\rho_N={\sigma\over\sigma_r^\star\sqrt{N_1}}
\le {\sigma\over cn^{3/2}},
\qquad
\rho_T\le {\sigma\over cn^{3/2}}.
\tag{9}
\]

The last row of \(\overline U\) has Euclidean norm at most \(\|\ell\|_2\), by (4), and the last row of \(\overline V\) has norm at most \(\|q\|_2\).  Therefore the target local-incoherence quantities defined in \(4.4\mathrm{a}\) satisfy
\[
\mu_{n+1}=\sqrt{{n+1\over r}}\,\|\overline U_{n+1,\boldsymbol\cdot}\|_2
\le {\sqrt2 B\over c},
\qquad
\nu_{n+1}\le {\sqrt2 B\over c}.
\tag{10}
\]
Combining (9)--(10), the two left sides in \(4.4\mathrm{b}\) are bounded by
\[
\max\{\mu_{n+1}\rho_T,\nu_{n+1}\rho_N\}\sqrt r
\le {\sqrt2 B\sigma\sqrt{r_0}\over c^2n^{3/2}}
\longrightarrow0
\tag{11}
\]
and
\[
\min\left\{{\mu_{n+1}\over\sqrt{N_1}},
{\nu_{n+1}\over\sqrt{T_1}}\right\}
\sqrt{r\log(N+T)}
\le {\sqrt2B\sqrt{r_0\log(2n+2)}\over c\sqrt n}
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{12}
\]
This proves \(4.4\mathrm{a}\)--\(4.4\mathrm{b}\) uniformly.

For every execution of \(H_n^{\mathrm{cert}}\), attach to each scalar, vector, or matrix node \(x\) a computed center \(\widehat x\) and a nonnegative outward radius \(r(x)\) in the absolute value, Euclidean norm, Frobenius norm, or operator norm specified for that node.  Observation inputs have their coordinate-box radii, and exact-dyadic public controls have radius zero.  For every directed scalar operation \(j\), choose the stored integer exponent \(e_j\) so that the magnitude of its exact result is at most \(2^{e_j}\), assign the outward rounding radius \(2^{e_j-q_n}\), and let \(\omega_q(x)\) be the sum of these radii transported to the norm of node \(x\) by the corresponding dimension factor.  Thus \(\omega_q(x)\) is observable and, when all intermediate magnitudes are at most \(M\), it is at most the operation count times a dimension factor times \(\eta_n(1+M)\), where \(\eta_n=2^{1-q_n}\).  Use
\[
r(x\mathbin\pm y)=r(x)+r(y)+\omega_q(x\mathbin\pm y),
\]
\[
r(xy)=\|\widehat x\|r(y)+\|\widehat y\|r(x)+r(x)r(y)+\omega_q(xy),
\]
and, for a scalar function \(g\) on an interval \(J\) containing its input,
\[
r(g(x))=\sup_{z\in J}|g'(z)|r(x)+\omega_q(g(x)).
\]
For inversion, if a computed \(L\) and an input enclosure of \(K\) satisfy
\[
\varrho(K,L):=\|I-\widehat K L\|+r(K)\|L\|<1,
\]
use
\[
r(K^{-1})={\|L\|\varrho(K,L)\over1-\varrho(K,L)}+\omega_q(K^{-1}).
\]
For a matrix-sign step \(S^+=(S+S^{-1})/2\), use
\[
r(S^+)={1\over2}\{r(S)+r(S^{-1})\}+\omega_q(S^+).
\]
All products forming invariant projectors, the retained pseudoinverse, and the endpoints use the same product rule.  A quantile is returned only as a certified probability-bracketing interval; a gate comparison is accepted or rejected only when its full enclosure lies on one side of the threshold, and otherwise the output is the outward hull of all feasible branches.  Precision doubling recomputes these recurrences and stops either at a certified sharp branch or at the prescribed coarse-hull cap.  These rules certify every returned enclosure by induction.  On any box for which every donor matrix \(X'\) satisfies \(s_r(X')\ge3cn/4\), \(s_{r+1}(X')\le cn/4\), and \(s_1(X')\le3C_0n/2\), the sharp branch is certified and every final radius is at most a fixed polynomial in \(n+T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+\alpha^{-1}+1\) times \(2^{-p_n}+2^{1-q_n}\). added_lemmas.proof_tex:
We first prove enclosure correctness.  Suppose \(\|x-\widehat x\|\le r(x)\) and \(\|y-\widehat y\|\le r(y)\).  The triangle inequality gives the addition rule.  Expanding a product gives
\[
xy-\widehat x\widehat y
=\widehat x(y-\widehat y)+(x-\widehat x)\widehat y
+(x-\widehat x)(y-\widehat y),
\]
so submultiplicativity gives exactly the displayed product radius before the nonnegative outward rounding term is added.  Correct rounding of a \(q_n\)-bit normalized significand changes a scalar result whose magnitude is at most \(2^{e_j}\) by less than one unit in its last place, hence by at most \(2^{e_j-q_n}\).  The triangle inequality over the scalar operations and \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm F}\) prove the asserted observable formula for \(\omega_q\).  The mean-value theorem gives the scalar-function rule.  These arguments apply entrywise or in any stated submultiplicative matrix norm.

For inversion, write \(R=I-KL\).  The hypotheses and the input enclosure give
\[
\|R\|
\le\|I-\widehat K L\|+\|K-\widehat K\|\|L\|
\le\varrho(K,L)<1.
\tag{1}
\]
The finite geometric identity
\[
(I-R)\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}R^j=I-R^m
\]
and \(\|R^m\|\le\|R\|^m\to0\) prove, without an external inversion theorem, that
\[
(I-R)^{-1}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}R^j,
\qquad
\|(I-R)^{-1}-I\|\le{\|R\|\over1-\|R\|}.
\tag{2}
\]
Since \(KL=I-R\), one has \(K^{-1}=L(I-R)^{-1}\).  Equations (1)--(2) therefore imply
\[
\|K^{-1}-L\|
\le {\|L\|\varrho(K,L)\over1-\varrho(K,L)},
\]
which is the inversion recurrence.  Applying the already proved addition and scaling rules to \((S+S^{-1})/2\) proves the matrix-sign recurrence.  Induction over the finite computation graph now proves every arithmetic enclosure.  Probability bisection preserves a bracket because a comparison is made only when the directed interval for the distribution function is wholly above or below the target probability.  Taking a hull when comparisons overlap contains every branch value.  Recomputing at a higher precision does not invalidate the last certified enclosure.  Thus adaptive branching and interval wrapping are sound.

It remains to prove the quantitative stable-box assertion rather than assuming it.  Put \(\tau=(cn/2)^2\).  On the stable box, the spectra of \(X^{\mathsf T}X-\tau I\) and \(XX^{\mathsf T}-\tau I\) are separated from zero by at least
\[
\min\left\{(3cn/4)^2-(cn/2)^2,
(cn/2)^2-(cn/4)^2\right\}
={3c^2n^2\over16}.
\tag{3}
\]
Their norms are at most a fixed multiple of \(n^2\).  After division by a certified power of two between that norm and twice that norm, every eigenvalue lies in
\[
[-1,-\gamma]\cup[\gamma,1]
\tag{4}
\]
for a fixed \(\gamma>0\) depending only on \(c,C_0\).  For a nonzero scalar \(x\), let \(s=\operatorname{sign}(x)\) and \(z=(x-s)/(x+s)\).  Direct substitution into \(x^+=(x+x^{-1})/2\) gives
\[
{x^+-s\over x^++s}=z^2.
\tag{5}
\]
Functional calculus for a real symmetric matrix and (4)--(5) show that after \(j\) exact sign iterations,
\[
\|S_j-\operatorname{sign}(S_0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le {2\chi^{2^j}\over1-\chi^{2^j}},
\qquad
\chi={1-\gamma\over1+\gamma}<1.
\tag{6}
\]
Thus \(O(\log(q_n+2))\) iterations make the truncation error at most \(2^{-q_n}\).  At the first step the inverse norm is at most \(\gamma^{-1}\), and thereafter every exact scalar iterate has absolute value at least one.  Hence the inverse residual test (1) succeeds once its input radius and rounding error are below a fixed constant.  The recurrence then bounds the accumulated sign radius by a fixed polynomial in \(n\) and the input magnitude times \(2^{-p_n}+2^{1-q_n}\); after the first step the derivative factor is at most one, and the number of remaining steps is logarithmic.  This rules out exponential wrapping growth.

The coordinate box gives
\[
\|X_1-X_2\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2n\,2^{-p_n-1},
\quad
\|R_1-R_2\|_2,\|C_1-C_2\|_2
\le2\sqrt n\,2^{-p_n-1}.
\tag{7}
\]
Equations (3)--(7) and the product recurrence therefore give projector radii bounded by a fixed polynomial times \(2^{-p_n}+2^{1-q_n}\).  The matrix
\[
K=X_rX_r^{\mathsf T}+I-P_L
\]
has eigenvalues at least \((3cn/4)^2\) on the retained space and eigenvalue one on its orthogonal complement.  Its inverse candidate passes (1), and the inversion and product recurrences applied to
\[
X_r^+=X_r^{\mathsf T}K^{-1}
\tag{8}
\]
give the same polynomial-times-\((2^{-p_n}+2^{1-q_n})\) bound.  Equations (6) and (8) use only the full spectral projector, so repeated singular values inside the retained cluster do not affect the argument.

On the stable box,
\[
{2\over3C_0n}\le\|X_r^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le{4\over3cn}.
\tag{9}
\]
All divisions in the analytic half-width are therefore by quantities bounded below by an inverse polynomial.  The arguments of its logarithms and square roots are at least one.  On the relevant probability range, the Gaussian and fixed-degree chi-square densities are positive.  For \(z>0\), integration of \(-\phi'(x)=x\phi(x)\) gives
\[
\int_z^\infty\phi(x)\,dx\le{\phi(z)\over z}.
\]
The Gaussian tail probability in \(\zeta_\alpha\) lies between \(3\alpha/8\) and \(\alpha/2\), and its quantile is bounded away from zero because \(\alpha<1/2\).  Hence the reciprocal Gaussian density is \(O(\alpha^{-1})\).  For the chi-square law, repeated integration by parts gives
\[
F_{\chi^2_{2r}}(x)=1-e^{-x/2}\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}{(x/2)^j\over j!}.
\tag{10}
\]
Its upper tail divided by its density is a polynomial of degree at most \(r-1\) in \(x\) and \(x^{-1}\).  Since \(r\le r_0\), the relevant upper-tail probability is at least \(\alpha/[4(1+t)]\), and \(t\) is bounded by a polynomial in \(n+T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+1\); formula (10) also bounds its quantile by a fixed multiple of \(1+\log(4(1+t)/\alpha)\).  Thus the reciprocal chi-square density is bounded by a polynomial in \(n+T_n^{\mathrm{enc}}+\alpha^{-1}+1\).  Certified probability bisection and the scalar recurrence consequently have polynomial condition factors.  Combining (7)--(10) with the finite endpoint computation proves the asserted polynomial-times-\((2^{-p_n}+2^{1-q_n})\) final radius.

Exact-dyadic controls have input radius zero.  For a certified control interval, its midpoint differs from every represented value by no more than half its width, so assigning that half-width as the initial radius makes the same induction valid.  This proves correctness but supplies no bound on the cost of producing successively smaller intervals.  Such a bound follows only after a uniform time-and-output-size modulus is given and included in the schedule and bit count, exactly as stated.

\quad\hbox{in \(L^1(P_n)\) and in probability},
\qquad
{\operatorname{length}(I_n^{\mathrm{fp}})
\over2\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)a_n}\longrightarrow1
\quad\hbox{in probability}.
\]
Finally, uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_n\), the expectation of every nonnegative recorded summand of \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{enc}}\) and \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{arith}}\), the fallback contribution \(M_0\mathbf1\{\kappa_n=1\}\), and \(\varepsilon_n\) is \(o(n^{-1})\).  In particular this holds along every sequence with \(r=1\) and \(u=v=0\).  No corresponding polynomial-complexity assertion is made for an arbitrary refinable public-control name unless a known uniform time-and-output-size modulus is incorporated into \(L_n\) and the schedule.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(\delta\) and an interior sequence \(P_n=P_{A,u,v}\) satisfying the hypotheses of the theorem.  All quantities below may depend on \(n\).  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}exact\mbox{-}rank}\), take a compact singular value decomposition
\[
A=USV^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
D=S^{-1}.
\]
By \(\mathrm{ass{:}strong\mbox{-}spectrum}\), every diagonal entry of the \(r\)-by-\(r\) diagonal matrix \(S\) is positive.  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}row\mbox{-}span}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}column\mbox{-}span}\), the coordinates
\[
x=(uV)^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^r,
\qquad
y=U^{\mathsf T}v\in\mathbb R^r
\]
obey \(u=x^{\mathsf T}V^{\mathsf T}\) and \(v=Uy\).  Since the Moore--Penrose inverse of the displayed compact singular value decomposition is \(A^+=V D U^{\mathsf T}\), the target in the theorem satisfies
\[
\theta_n(P_n)=uA^+v=x^{\mathsf T}Dy. \tag{1}
\]
Thus this equality is a consequence of the span restrictions and the target definition, rather than a definition of an observed-law surrogate.  Orthonormality of the columns of \(U\) and \(V\), together with \(\mathrm{def{:}transition\mbox{-}scale}\), gives
\[
a_n=\sigma\bigl(\|Dx\|_2^2+\|Dy\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2},
\qquad
b_n=\sigma^2\|D\|_{\mathrm F},
\qquad
w_n=a_n+b_n. \tag{2}
\]
In particular, \(b_n>0\), because \(r\geq1\), \(\sigma>0\), and \(D\) has positive diagonal entries; hence division by \(w_n\) below is valid.

Put
\[
\tau=\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}.
\]
The restriction \(0<\alpha<1/2\) implies \(0<\tau<1/2\).  We construct alternatives by leaving \(A\) and the noise covariance fixed and perturbing only \((x,y)\).

First suppose \(a_n>0\).  For \(g(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}Dy\), direct differentiation gives
\[
\nabla g(x,y)=(Dy,Dx),
\qquad
\|\nabla g(x,y)\|_2=a_n/\sigma>0.
\]
Define \((h_x,h_y)=\sigma\tau\nabla g/\|\nabla g\|_2\).  For \(s\in\{-1,1\}\), let \(Q_s\) retain \(A\) and have coordinates \((x+s h_x,y+s h_y)\).  Expanding (1), its target displacement is
\[
\Delta_s
=\theta_n(Q_s)-\theta_n(P_n)
=s\{h_x^{\mathsf T}Dy+x^{\mathsf T}Dh_y\}+h_x^{\mathsf T}Dh_y
=s\tau a_n+h_x^{\mathsf T}Dh_y. \tag{3}
\]
For real \(z,c_0\), \(\max\{|z+c_0|,|-z+c_0|\}\geq |z|\), because otherwise the triangle inequality applied to their difference \(2z\) would fail.  Applying this fact to (3) yields
\[
\max_{s\in\{-1,1\}}|\Delta_s|\geq\tau a_n. \tag{4}
\]
When \(a_n=0\), (4) remains valid with zero right-hand side and no first-order alternatives are required.

For the second-order alternatives, choose \(j\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(D_{jj}=\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}\), and put \(h_0=\sigma\tau/\sqrt2\).  For each \((s,t)\in\{-1,1\}^2\), let \(Q_{s,t}\) retain \(A\) and have coordinates
\[
(x+s h_0e_j,\ y+t h_0e_j).
\]
Another expansion of (1) gives
\[
\Delta_{s,t}
=\theta_n(Q_{s,t})-\theta_n(P_n)
=s h_0(Dy)_j+t h_0(Dx)_j+st h_0^2D_{jj}. \tag{5}
\]
Multiplication by \(st\) and averaging over the four signs cancels the two linear terms, so
\[
\frac14\sum_{s,t\in\{-1,1\}}st\Delta_{s,t}
=h_0^2D_{jj}
=\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{2}\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}. \tag{6}
\]
The absolute value of the left side of (6) is at most \(\max_{s,t}|\Delta_{s,t}|\).  Also, because \(D\) has \(r\leq r_0\) diagonal entries,
\[
\|D\|_{\mathrm F}^2=\sum_{k=1}^rD_{kk}^2
\leq r\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
\leq r_0\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2.
\]
Equations (2) and (6) therefore imply
\[
\max_{s,t\in\{-1,1\}}|\Delta_{s,t}|
\geq\frac{\tau^2}{2\sqrt{r_0}}b_n. \tag{7}
\]

We now verify both model membership and locality, including the boundary constraints needed for those conclusions.  Any coordinate perturbation \((q_x,q_y)\) used above is implemented by
\[
u'=u+q_x^{\mathsf T}V^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
v'=v+Uq_y. \tag{8}
\]
It preserves \(u'\in\operatorname{row}(A)\) and \(v'\in\operatorname{col}(A)\).  For every first- or second-order alternative,
\[
\|q_x\|_2^2+\|q_y\|_2^2=\sigma^2\tau^2. \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, this is immediate from the normalization of \((h_x,h_y)\) in the first case and from \(2h_0^2=\sigma^2\tau^2\) in the second.  By the theorem's interior incoherence condition and \(r\leq r_0\), (8)--(9) give, for every coordinate \(k\),
\[
\bigl|q_x^{\mathsf T}V_{k\mathbin{\boldsymbol\cdot}}^{\mathsf T}\bigr|
\leq\|q_x\|_2\|V_{k\mathbin{\boldsymbol\cdot}}\|_2
\leq\sigma\tau\sqrt{\frac{\mu r_0}{n}},
\qquad
\bigl|(Uq_y)_k\bigr|
\leq\sigma\tau\sqrt{\frac{\mu r_0}{n}}. \tag{10}
\]
The class constants \(\sigma,\mu,r_0\) and the positive slack \(\delta\) are fixed, so the last bound is at most \(\delta\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).  Since the interior hypothesis gives \(\|u\|_\infty,\|v\|_\infty\leq B-\delta\), (10) implies \(\|u'\|_\infty,\|v'\|_\infty\leq B\).  The matrix \(A\) is unchanged, so its exact rank, spectral bounds, singular spaces, incoherence, and entry bound continue to satisfy respectively \(\mathrm{ass{:}exact\mbox{-}rank}\), \(\mathrm{ass{:}strong\mbox{-}spectrum}\), \(\mathrm{ass{:}incoherence}\), and \(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\mbox{-}entries}\).  The covariance is unchanged and satisfies \(\mathrm{ass{:}gaussian\mbox{-}blocks}\).  Thus every constructed alternative belongs to \(\mathcal P_n\) by \(\mathrm{def{:}model\mbox{-}class}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).

Orthonormality in (8) and (9) yield
\[
\|u-u'\|_2^2+\|v-v'\|_2^2
=\|q_x\|_2^2+\|q_y\|_2^2
=\sigma^2\tau^2.
\]
Because \(A\) is unchanged, \(\mathrm{def{:}local\mbox{-}neighborhood}\) now gives
\[
\operatorname{KL}(P_n,Q)=\frac{\tau^2}{2}<1 \tag{11}
\]
for every constructed alternative \(Q\).  Hence all of them lie in \(\mathcal N_n(P_n)\).

We next derive the probability comparison used below directly from \(\mathrm{ass{:}gaussian\mbox{-}blocks}\).  For any constructed \(Q\), the joint data densities \(p\) and \(q\) under \(P_n\) and \(Q\) are Gaussian with common covariance \(\sigma^2I\), and (9) says that their mean vectors are separated by Euclidean norm \(\sigma\tau\).  Completing the square in the Gaussian densities gives
\[
\int\sqrt{pq}=\exp(-\tau^2/8).
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz and \(1-e^{-z}\leq z\) for \(z\geq0\) then give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{TV}(P_n,Q)
&=\frac12\int|\sqrt p-\sqrt q\,|\,(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)\\
&\leq\frac12
\left\{\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\right\}^{1/2}
\left\{\int(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)^2\right\}^{1/2}\\
&=\sqrt{1-\left(\int\sqrt{pq}\right)^2}
=\sqrt{1-e^{-\tau^2/4}}
\leq\frac\tau2. 
\end{aligned} \tag{12}
\]

Define
\[
\gamma_n=\inf_{H\in\mathcal P_n}H\{\theta_n(H)\in J_n\},
\qquad
\varepsilon_n=(1-\alpha-\gamma_n)_+.
\]
The assumed lower limit for uniform coverage implies \(\varepsilon_n\to0\), and the definition of the infimum implies, for every \(H\in\mathcal P_n\),
\[
H\{\theta_n(H)\in J_n\}\geq1-\alpha-\varepsilon_n. \tag{13}
\]
For any constructed alternative \(Q\), total-variation transfer of the second event in (13), followed by the union bound under \(P_n\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
&P_n\{\theta_n(P_n)\in J_n,\ \theta_n(Q)\in J_n\}\\
&\quad\geq
P_n\{\theta_n(P_n)\in J_n\}
+P_n\{\theta_n(Q)\in J_n\}-1\\
&\quad\geq1-2\alpha-2\varepsilon_n-\operatorname{TV}(P_n,Q)\\
&\quad\geq1-2\alpha-2\varepsilon_n-\frac\tau2. 
\end{aligned} \tag{14}
\]
On this event the interval contains both real numbers, so its length is at least \(|\theta_n(Q)-\theta_n(P_n)|\).

Choose \(Q_n^\star\) from the finite union of the required first-order alternatives and the four second-order alternatives to maximize absolute displacement.  Equations (4) and (7) show, also when \(a_n=0\), that
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\theta_n(Q_n^\star)-\theta_n(P_n)|
&\geq\max\left\{\tau a_n,\frac{\tau^2}{2\sqrt{r_0}}b_n\right\}\\
&\geq\frac{\tau^2}{4\sqrt{r_0}}(a_n+b_n)
=\frac{\tau^2}{4\sqrt{r_0}}w_n. 
\end{aligned} \tag{15}
\]
For the second inequality, \(\max\{z_1,z_2\}\geq(z_1+z_2)/2\) for nonnegative \(z_1,z_2\), and \(\tau/2\geq\tau^2/(4\sqrt{r_0})\) because \(0<\tau<1/2\) and \(r_0\geq1\).

Combining (14)--(15), with the conclusion automatic if the expected length is infinite, gives
\[
\frac{\mathbb E_{P_n}[\operatorname{length}(J_n)]}{w_n(P_n)}
\geq
\frac{\tau^2}{4\sqrt{r_0}}
\left(1-2\alpha-2\varepsilon_n-\frac\tau2\right). \tag{16}
\]
Finally, \(P_n\in\mathcal N_n(P_n)\) because \(\operatorname{KL}(P_n,P_n)=0\) in \(\mathrm{def{:}local\mbox{-}neighborhood}\).  Therefore the supremum over \(Q\in\mathcal N_n(P_n)\) in the theorem is at least the left side of (16).  Taking lower limits, using \(\varepsilon_n\to0\), and substituting \(\tau=(1-2\alpha)/2\), proves the asserted bound with the explicit fixed-class constant
\[
k_\alpha
=\frac{\tau^2}{4\sqrt{r_0}}
\left(1-2\alpha-\frac\tau2\right)
=\frac{3\tau^2(1-2\alpha)}{16\sqrt{r_0}}>0.
\]
